01 The problem: a result without understanding
A patient leaves the laboratory with a panel of unfamiliar terms and units:
PDW
Platelet distribution width
MCHC
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration
Monocyte
One type of white blood cell
G/L
Giga (10⁹) cells per litre
fL
Femtolitre, a unit of cell volume
pg
Picogram, a unit of mass
The reference interval is printed beside each value, so a patient can see that a number falls outside it, but not what it measures or what to do next.
60.3%
of older adults in Da Nang have inadequate general health literacy
46%
of patients search online to understand their own test results
Sources: cross-sectional study in Da Nang (n = 204 older adults); Giardina et al., JAMIA 2018 (n = 93)

02 How patients currently close the gap
They photograph the report and ask a general-purpose language model.
PROMPT
“Briefly explain what white blood cells are” (asked in Vietnamese)
3B MODEL RESPONSE (translated; errors underlined)
“White blood cells … are lymphocytes capable of moving through the blood … They help the body fight viruses, bacteria and cancer-causing cells. When the immune system is weakened, white blood cells also decrease …”
① Definitional error
Lymphocytes are one type of white blood cell, not a synonym.
② Unprompted disease
Raises cancer and immune deficiency without being asked.
A patient with an entirely normal result meets one definitional error and two alarming diseases in a single short answer.

03 But the most dangerous failure runs the other way
Terminological error
Visible to the reader, and invites verification with a doctor.
Risk: lower — the reader notices it
False reassurance
Fluent and comfortable, and removes the reason to seek care.
Risk: higher — the reader trusts it
Definition — false reassurance: asserting that all results are normal on a panel that is NOT normal.
ACTUAL OUTPUT FROM OUR EXPERIMENT · PANEL LABELLED “SEEK CARE”
“All test results are within the normal range.”
→ We treat this as a distinct error class and measure it separately.

04 Four-layer architecture
Principle: NO clinical judgement is delegated to the language model.
LAYER 1
Normalisation
Name → canonical code
Unit conversion
■ No LLM
[icon: arrow-right]
LAYER 2
Rule-based labelling
Compare to reference interval
Assign 3-level label
■ No LLM
[icon: arrow-right]
LAYER 3
Constrained generation
Model receives the labels
Paraphrases only
● LLM
[icon: arrow-right]
LAYER 4
Validation
Check text against labels
Regenerate / template
■ No LLM
3-level labels (Layer 2):
Normal · inside interval
Monitor · slightly outside
Seek care · far outside
Panel label = most severe analyte
Failing output → regenerate → fixed template after the retry limit. Unverified text is never displayed.

05 Layer 1 — Name and unit normalisation
One analyte, many names
WBC
SLBC
Số lượng bạch cầu
* WBC
↓ all map to one canonical code: white blood cell count
Markers % and # separate a percentage from an absolute count, and may precede (% Neu) or follow (NEUT%) the name.
Units are the serious problem
Report: Hb = 14.56 g/dL
Interval: 130–175 g/L
✗ Unconverted → classified “SEEK CARE” (false alarm)
✓ Converted → 145.6 g/L → Normal
Hb = haemoglobin · 1 g/dL = 10 g/L
Rule: unknown or missing unit → REFUSE to process. Never guess.
External evidence: 6–19% of laboratory tests cannot be accurately mapped to LOINC (the international code standard for lab tests); an analysis of 163 million results identified 2,019 distinct unit expressions.

06 Layers 3 & 4 — Constrained generation and validation
Layer 3 · Three constraints
① Input
The model is GIVEN labels, never asked to derive them
② Content
No disease names, causes, medications or dosages
③ Output
Fixed JSON schema required (machine-checkable)
Layer 4 · Six error classes checked
1 Direction — does high/low match the Layer 2 label?
2 Contradiction — does the prose contradict the label?
3 Forbidden terms — are any present?
4 Fabrication — is any analyte invented?
5 Omission — is any analyte left out?
6 False reassurance — does the closing falsely reassure?
Model: Qwen2.5-3B served locally via Ollama — data never leaves the institution, no GPU required.
Qwen2.5-3B: open language model, 3 billion parameters · Ollama: tool for running models on a local machine

07 Evaluation design
Dataset
  • 150 synthetic complete blood count panels
  • 10–18 analytes per panel
  • Equally split across 3 severity classes
  • Random aliases and units per analyte
Why synthetic data
  • Ground-truth labels required; real reports carry none
  • Balanced design required; real panels are mostly normal
  • No patient data handled
Three configurations compared
baseline
Raw values given to the model. No labels, no constraints, no validation.
Layers used: none (LLM only)
constrained
Labels and constraints, but output not verified.
Layers used: L1 · L2 · L3
full
Complete, with regeneration and template fallback.
Layers used: L1 · L2 · L3 · L4

Safe output: verified text shown to patient
Model pass: model text passed, no template needed
False reassur.: “all normal” on an abnormal panel
Direction mismatch: high/low opposite to the label
Contradict. wording: prose contradicts the label
Forbidden terms: disease, cause, drug or dose
Fabricated: analyte not in the panel is mentioned
Omitted: analyte in the panel is left out
Every error metric decreases monotonically: baseline → constrained → full.

09 Three key findings
32% → 0%
False reassurance
Unconstrained: roughly one patient in three with abnormal results would be told nothing needed attention.
91.3% → 0%
Direction mismatch
The model judging for itself fails almost always. Moved to a rule layer, classification becomes exact.
48%
Constraints insufficient
Only 48% of prompt-constrained outputs passed; over half failed validation. Instruction does not guarantee compliance.
IMPORTANT CAVEAT
The 100% safe output = 64% model-generated text + 36% fixed templates. The guarantee comes from the pipeline, and is not evidence that a 3B model performs this task reliably.

10 Discussion — two observations
1
False reassurance deserves its own metric
Current evaluations report readability and factual accuracy. A falsely reassuring sentence may still score HIGH on readability, because it is simple and calming. The harm: it stops the reader from seeking care.
2
Unit standardisation is a safety precondition
The unit error occurred inside the rule layer, the layer treated as exact. No downstream validation detects it, because every later layer faithfully reproduces a confidently wrong label.
Data standardisation (LOINC, HL7 FHIR) is therefore a precondition for rule-based clinical logic, not only a data-reuse concern.
LOINC: standard codes for lab tests · HL7 FHIR: standard for exchanging health data

11 Limitations
① No clinical validation
All evaluation is automated. No medical professional reviewed the generated explanations.
→ Next: review by medical professionals
② Thresholds not grounded
Severity factors separating “monitor” from “seek care” were set heuristically, not against a critical value list.
→ Next: use a laboratory critical value list
③ Synthetic data
Real reports carry noise, missing fields and formatting variation this study does not capture.
→ Next: real reports from multiple laboratories
④ Narrow scope
Complete blood count only. No biochemistry, one-sided intervals, qualitative results, or OCR (reading photos of reports).
→ Next: biochemistry and qualitative results

12 Conclusion and future work
The language model is not permitted to judge whether a value is abnormal. Rules decide first, the model paraphrases, a validator checks one against the other.

Future work, in order of importance
1 Clinical validation by medical professionals most pressing
2 Replace heuristic thresholds with a critical value list
3 Extend to biochemistry and qualitative results
4 Speech output layer for elderly and low-literacy patients
5 Evaluation on real reports from multiple laboratories
